analysis.one_liner: Penalizes companies that move call center jobs overseas and makes them disclose where agents are located.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote; it sat in four House committees until Congress ended with no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a public list of employers that close US call centers and move the work overseas, and cut those employers off from federal grants and federally backed loans for five years. It would have required federal contracts to keep call center work in the US, given a contracting preference to companies that don't offshore, and made any company whose agents are located overseas tell consumers the agent's location at the start of a customer service call — with a right to be transferred to a US-based agent. The FTC would enforce the disclosure rules, and companies failing to notify the Labor Department before offshoring could face fines up to $10,000 per day.
analysis.who_benefits: US call center workers, who would face a new federal deterrent to having their jobs moved overseas, plus consumers, who would know whether they were speaking with an agent abroad and could demand a US-based agent. Companies that keep call center work in the US would gain a contracting preference.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US call center workers and consumers

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 50 or more call center employees would have to notify the Labor Department 120 days before moving call center work overseas, and violators could face a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per day.

The Labor Department would publish a public list of companies that relocate or contract out call center work overseas, and those companies would be barred from federal grants and federally guaranteed loans for five years, with waivers only for national security, US job loss, or environmental harm.

Call center work performed under civilian or defense federal contracts would have to be done inside the United States, and agencies would give contracting preference to employers not on the offshoring list.

Businesses whose customer service agents are located outside the US would have to have each agent disclose their physical location at the start of a customer service call, and consumers could request transfer to an agent located in the US; the FTC would enforce this under its deceptive-practices authority.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that offshore call center work — they would face fines, a public blacklist, five-year ineligibility for federal grants and guaranteed loans, and a loss of federal contracting preference. Businesses generally would bear compliance costs for location disclosure and annual FTC certification, and consumers could indirectly pay through somewhat higher service costs if offshoring savings shrink.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies that offshore call center jobs

drawbacks.text: The disclosure, transfer, and annual certification requirements impose compliance costs on every business that runs customer service lines, including companies whose agents are all already in the US, which must still certify compliance to the FTC each year.

Restricting federal grants and guaranteed loans for listed companies is a blunt instrument: a company could lose access to federal funding for a single relocation decision, and waiver exceptions require case-by-case determinations by the Secretary of Labor.

Companies would argue that offshoring customer service keeps prices lower for consumers, so shrinking the offshoring cost advantage could translate into higher prices or fees for the same consumers the bill protects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — a public deterrent to offshoring call center jobs and transparency for consumers about who they are talking to — are real and modestly priced for the public. The main costs fall on businesses that offshore, in the form of lost federal funding access and compliance burdens, and the annual certification requirement applies broadly. A good-faith concern is that reducing offshoring savings could raise consumer prices, but the bill's core tradeoff is deliberately making it more expensive to move US service jobs abroad.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to four House committees, but none of them ever scheduled a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Sharice Davids of Kansas introduced the bill on May 8, 2024, together with Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican.
The same day, the Speaker sent the bill to four committees: Energy and Commerce, plus Education and the Workforce, Oversight, and Armed Services, each holding only the portions in its jurisdiction.
On May 17, 2024, the Energy and Commerce Committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce; no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.
The bill had 25 cosponsors — 24 Democrats and 1 Republican — but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that move or contract out call center work overseas are better off: they remain fully eligible for federal grants and guaranteed loans, keep the federal contracting status quo, and face no disclosure requirement about where their service agents are located. US workers who lost call center jobs to offshoring get no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that offshore call center work

for.name: Rep. Sharice Davids
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 8, 2024, the lead author of the offshoring penalties and disclosure requirements.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Joined Davids in introducing the bill, making it bipartisan at introduction.

for.name: 25 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, but no cosponsor chaired a committee that acted on the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 8, 2024, sent it to subcommittee on May 17, and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce, Oversight, and Armed Services Committees
against.what_they_did: Held their portions of the bill for consideration and took no action during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic — 24 of 25 cosponsors — with one Republican, Rep. Fitzpatrick, as an original sponsor; with no vote ever taken, no broader pattern of support or opposition was recorded.

industries.industry: Overseas call center and outsourcing firms (offshore BPO industry)
industries.note: The bill attacks their core business model: companies that contract call center work overseas would be publicly listed and their US employers would lose federal grants and loan guarantees for five years. Demand for offshore call centers would shrink.

industries.industry: US companies that offshore customer service (telecom, banking, retail, tech)
industries.note: These companies profit today by running service operations abroad at lower cost; the bill would make that choice costly — fines up to $10,000 per day for failing to notify, loss of federal funding access, and mandatory disclosure that agents are overseas with a consumer right to a US agent.

industries.industry: US-based call centers and domestic customer service operations
industries.note: Federal contracting preference and the ban on offshored work under federal contracts would steer government call center demand to US-based operations, supporting domestic jobs.
